There is one way to do it where it isn't awful for the environment. Use liquid nitrogen for the fracking fluid instead of diesel fuel. The liquid nitrogen boils off into regular nitrogen which makes up around 70% of the air we breathe. It does cost more on the front end to frack this way, though that cost is made up on the back end by not having to spend any money to clean up any pollution. That being said, there aren't that many companies using this method. Make of that what you will.
Does the act of 'mining' this stuff hurt the ecosystem much?

When they first place the rigs, they have to clear a relatively large area of land, but once the rig is placed it grows back fairly quickly. It might take up as much land area as a water tower, or cell phone tower. There also has to be a retention pond to hold the fracking fluid used to shatter the rock when nitrogen isn't used. There are other issues, such as destablization of the bedrock, since the oil shales are literally shattered to allow oil and natural gas to flow.

What always gets me about this is that it is much cleaner to use liquid nitrogen as the fracking fluid. It's more expensive than using diesel fuel and whatever proprietary chemicals each company uses until you account for the cleanup costs. Nitrogen cost about the same as using other fracking fluids since the cleanup costs are less. What this means is that there is an incentive to use diesel if you aren't planning on cleaning up.
